newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Lehman sees more energy M&A, ventures.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Lehman sees more energy M&A, ventures.

text.p: The rate of merger and joint venture activity in the U.S. energy industry is set to accelerate as many companies have gone as far as they can with internal cost-cutting, a leading adviser in the field said.

"Their choice now is either to grow through getting a bigger slice of the pie or quit areas where they cannot compete and focus on what they do best," Grant Porter, managing director at Lehman Brothers global natural resource group, said in an interview Friday.

The U.S. downstream sector -- energy-refining and marketing -- has already experienced a raft of joint venture and mergers involving some of the world's biggest oil companies, such as Royal Dutch/Shell Group with Texaco Inc, British Petroleum Co Plc with Mobil Corp, and Ultramar Diamond Shamrock with Total Petroleum (North America).

Lehman is currently advising USX-Marathon Group in its downstream joint venture with Ashland Inc. "That is a prototypical deal, both companies were profitable but found that return on capital was not adequate," Porter said.

Similar partnerships have generated greater dividends than initially anticipated. In May, BP increased its forecast of savings from its Mobil venture to $500 million a year. This week, Valero said its Basis acquisition would contribute $20 million in the second quarter. And analysts say the Marathon-Ashland deal could generate savings and revenue enhancements of $100 million to $200 million a year.

In the upstream sector, there has been a spate of asset sales and mergers as companies seek to work out how best to deal with a cyclical commodity business in which oil prices linger in a range of $18-$20 a barrel.
However, despite the hostile offer by Union Pacific Resources Group Inc for Pennzoil Co earlier this week, Porter does not see a trend toward more unfriendly activity.
As Lehman is advising Pennzoil on its defence, he could not talk specifically on that bid but noted that such offers were extremely difficult to carry out.
"Hostile bids are very difficult to do as you do not have the same information as an agreed merger, you will always have to pay the full price and there is no shortage of white knights," Porter said.

His partner, Skip McGee, doubted there would be a proliferation of unfriendly bids in the sector, although he said a few people, such as J.P, Bryan at Gulf Canada Resources Ltd, would continue to get hostile deals done.

Analysts say one problem with Union Pacific's offer is the earnings per share dilution of 50 percent that the company said it would experience as a result of the deal, although it did say the transaction would immediately add to cash flow per share.
Investors are unlikely to be happy when hostile bids give rise to that sort of situation, Porter said.
"There is always going to be earnings per share dilution when you buy upstream companies for cash," he said.
More likely are deals such as Amoco Corp's sale of 15 percent of its U.S. reserves, which the company has said attracted a lot of interest from independent exploration and production companies.

Porter also pointed out that a company such as Shell had not stopped at a single deal. After going into the Gulf of Mexico, Shell struck a downstream deal with Texaco and upstream deals with Amoco and Mobil.

For the independent oil and gas producers, Porter expects the trend of friendly mergers to continue. Lehman advised MESA Inc on its recapitalization, which led to an agreed merger with Parker & Parsley Petroleum Co.
"Given where the stock market is, it is hard to say that it is cheaper to find reserves on Wall Street," Porter said.
In natural gas distribution and other so-called midstream activities, the rationale for joint ventures is slightly different from the cost-cutting that has propelled downstream mergers.
"People are looking for synergies and they need to have a critical mass to capture high-margin opportunities in an environment where margins overall are shrinking," Grant said.
Among others, Lehman advised PanEnergy Corp in its merger with Duke Energy Corp, Valero Energy Corp on its deal with PG&E Corp and TPC Corp in its deal with PacifiCorp.
"Natural gas companies are starting to get together with electric utilities as utilities look to gas companies to help them learn to compete in a deregulated market," Porter said.
((-- David Chance New York Newsroom 212 859 1902))
